place: A dry-stone well shaft on an abandoned holding, some ten fathoms deep, covered for years with a slab and never drawn from.
lines: tie the lamp to the rope and lower it down the well
watch the flame as it goes
things: heavy stale air pooled at the bottom
rotting leaves and a little black water at the bottom
outcome: The lamp burns steadily for most of the way down, then the flame shrinks to a blue bead and goes out a couple of fathoms above the bottom. Hauled up, the lamp is unharmed and relights at once in the open. The player now knows a person climbing down would grow dizzy and drop in the same place, but knows nothing about how to clear the air, and the bad air is still there tomorrow because nothing stirs it.

place: A worked-out level in an old tin mine, wet-walled, its roof held by round oak props and lid-boards set forty years ago and not inspected since.
things: a wheelbarrow left standing under the roof
outcome: Nobody is there. Damp and fungus have been softening the props at the foot for decades; through a wet winter one prop crushes at its base, its neighbours take the load and creak for days, and then two more fail together and a slab of roof the size of a cart comes down with its rubble. The level is blocked, the barrow is flattened, and dust hangs for an hour. The warning signs, props bulging and shedding splinters, a trickle of grit from the roof, were there for weeks for anyone who had come to look.

place: The lip of a pothole on a limestone moor, a black slot a stride wide whose bottom cannot be seen by daylight.

outcome: The stone falls clear for two breaths, cracks off a ledge, rattles, and ends in a deep plop. The player learns it is a long drop, more than a short rope, that it is not a clean shaft, and that there is standing water at the bottom, but the count is muddled by the ledge so the depth is a guess good to a few fathoms at best. The jackdaws burst out past the player's face. The stone is gone for good.

place: A miners' dry store cut into the side of an adit near the entrance, with a plank shelf, a box of tallow candles, a coil of greased rope and a sack of oat bread.
things: tallow candles in a wooden box
the miner who returns after five days
outcome: Rats find the store within a night or two. They eat the bread first, then gnaw through the corner of the candle box and eat the tallow candles down to a few stubs and loose wicks, and they chew the greased rope for its fat in several places without eating much of it. The tin tinderbox is untouched. The miner comes back to a store with no food, an hour or so of light instead of a week's, and a rope that looks whole in the coil but has strands bitten through in its middle.

place: A body-width rift in limestone, shoulder high, that narrows to a squeeze a hand's breadth wider than a man's chest before opening into a chamber.

outcome: With the pack on, the player jams at the chest and cannot go on or, for a bad minute, back. Pack off and pushed ahead, breath let out, they scrape through sideways in a few minutes, leaving a coat button and some skin behind. The lamp, held at arm's length and tipped while wriggling, spills a third of its oil and nearly goes out. Coming back the same way will be harder if they are tired, wet, or carrying anything they found.

place: A stream cave under a moor, entered by a dry crawl that dips to within a forearm of the stream before rising into larger passage beyond.
things: inner chamber with a high shelf
a person exploring the inner chamber

outcome: Heavy rain starts on the moor while the explorer is inside and knows nothing of it. The peat soaks it up for an hour or two, then the stream rises fast, turns brown and loud, and within half an hour of the first rise the low crawl is filled to the roof. The explorer is cut off in the inner chamber, safe on the high shelf but wet, cold and using up light, and must wait most of a day after the rain stops for the water to drop enough to pass. The only warnings were a change in the stream's sound, a cold draught dying, and foam arriving.

outcome: The lamp gives perhaps two hours on what is in it and the player has used one getting here. Going on, the flame shrinks and yellows as the oil gets low, and it dies on the way back with a third of the distance still to go. In total dark the tinderbox gives sparks but nothing to keep alight except the dry wick, which glows for a minute. The player must feel along one wall, slowly, and a journey of twenty minutes takes hours, with every junction a guess and the floor drop a real danger.

place: An earth-floored stone cellar under a farmhouse, cool all year, its walls sweating in summer, with one slatted shelf and iron hooks in the beams.
things: sack of wheat flour set on the earth floor
second sack of flour on the slatted shelf
the cook who opens the sacks six weeks later
outcome: Nothing happens that anyone sees. The sack on the floor draws damp up through the cloth; within a fortnight the bottom hand's depth of flour is caked, within six weeks it is grey, musty and crawling, and the taint has spread through half the sack. The sack on the shelf, with air under it, is sound apart from a slight cellar smell. The cook loses about half a sack and cannot tell from the outside of either sack which is which until a hand goes in.

place: A pitch of four fathoms inside a cave, with a sharp limestone lip at its head and a single stout stalagmite boss a few paces back from the edge.
lines: tie the rope round the stone pillar and climb down
climb back up
go down again for the second load
things: sacks of ore at the bottom
outcome: The anchor is good and the first descent and climb are fine. But every time weight comes on and off, the rope saws a finger's width back and forth over the lip, and hemp does not stand that: after the first trip a strand is furred, after the second it is cut half through at that one spot. On the third climb, loaded with a sack, it parts a fathom below the top. Folding the jerkin under the rope at the lip would have prevented all of it, and looking at that one hand's breadth of rope between trips would have shown it coming.

place: The dead end of a hand-cut copper level, the face hard quartzy rock that iron picks barely mark, a rill of water running in the floor gutter.
lines: stack the firewood against the rock face and light it

things: two barrow loads of dry split wood
leather buckets of water from the gutter
outcome: This is the old way and it works, slowly. The fire has to burn hard against the face for hours, and the level fills with smoke so nobody can stay in it until the next morning. Water thrown on the hot face makes it crack and spit scalding flakes and a rush of steam; afterwards a hand's depth of rock is shattered and comes away easily with pick and wedge. A day and a night and a cartload of wood buy about as much ground as a week of bare pick work, and the roof above the fire is loosened too and must be barred down before anyone works under it.

place: Rough hill grazing over limestone, with an open shaft a body wide hidden in bracken, and a spring line at the hill foot where the village draws water.
outcome: The ewe, grazing head down into the bracken, steps into the shaft and falls. She breaks a leg and lies bleating; the shepherd, two fields away, might hear it on a still evening and might not, and she dies in two or three days of thirst and injury. In warm weather the carcass is foul within the week, and rain washes it into the stream that feeds the spring. A fortnight after a sheep went missing, people in the village have griping bowels and nobody connects the two.

place: A dry upper chamber of a limestone cave, far from any stream, where a single stalactite drips steadily onto a knob of flowstone.
lines: put the cooking pot under the drip
sleep until it is full
things: iron cooking pot holding about two quarts
outcome: It works, at the drip's pace. A drop every couple of breaths is about a cupful an hour, so the pot is full after a night's sleep, not before, and a thirsty person gets a mouthful at a time if they cannot wait. The water is cold, clean and hard. The drop striking water in an iron pot rings all night in the quiet chamber, and the splash throws a fine spray, so a bedroll laid within arm's reach is damp along one edge by morning.

place: A village draw-well six fathoms to water with two fathoms of water in it, a wooden windlass over it, the water black and unseeable from above.
lines: lower the bucket and wind it up full

things: well rope with a worn knot

outcome: The worn knot slips as the full bucket comes off the water, and rope comes up empty. An oak bucket with iron hoops, once full, sinks and lies on the bottom on its side. Fishing blind with the grapple takes patience: most casts bring up nothing, some bring up a rotten rope end or a boot, and dragging fast only stirs mud. After half an hour of slow sweeps a prong catches the bail and the bucket comes up, or it catches a hoop and pulls it off, leaving staves on the bottom. The water is cloudy for the rest of the day either way.

place: A lead mine with two levels running side by side through solid rock some fathoms apart, one of them just closed by a fall.
things: a miner trapped beyond the fall
two rescuers in the neighbouring level
outcome: The trapped miner beats his hammer on the wall in threes. Rock carries a knock far better than air carries a shout, so the rescuers in the next level hear it clearly though they never heard him calling. They knock back and he answers, so both sides know someone is alive. But the sound seems to come from the whole wall at once: they can tell he is near, not where, and they argue whether to dig through the fall or drive across from their level. Counts of knocks can pass a number, how many men, and little more.
